name: Tourette's disorder
summary: Multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic lasting more than a year, beginning before age 18. Behavioral therapy (CBIT) is first-line for impairing tics. FDA-approved drugs are the dopamine-blocking antipsychotics haloperidol, pimozide, and aripiprazole; alpha-2 agonists are widely used off-label, especially with co-occurring ADHD. Ecopipam (a D1 antagonist) was under FDA priority review as of late 2026 and is not approved.
plainSummary: Tourette's causes repeated movements or sounds (tics) that a person can't fully control. Behavior therapy is often tried first, and a few medicines are approved to reduce tics when they cause real problems.

approved.drugClass: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic; dopamine D2 partial agonist
approved.indication: Treatment of Tourette's disorder in pediatric patients 6 to 18 years.

dosing.target: Under 50 kg: 5 mg/day after 2 days. 50 kg or more: 5 mg/day for days 3–7, then 10 mg/day on day 8.
dosing.max: 10 mg/day (under 50 kg); 20 mg/day (50 kg or more)
dosing.notes: Adjust at intervals of at least 1 week. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers: half the usual dose; adjust for strong CYP2D6/CYP3A4 inhibitors and CYP3A4 inducers.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors with antidepressant drugs (children, adolescents, and young adults)
approved.plainSummary: An antipsychotic medicine taken once a day that can reduce tics in children and teens; weight and blood sugar need monitoring.

verified.note: Abilify label effective 1/2025 and Opipza label (DailyMed setid b47ede68-8942-4432-af7e-57afc14b2ba4) checked; both list pediatric Tourette’s disorder. Opipza formulation-specific dosing may differ; consult its label.

brands: Haldol (oral brand discontinued; generic tablets and oral concentrate marketed)
approved.indication: Control of tics and vocal utterances of Tourette's Disorder in children and adults.

population.ages: Children 3 years and older and adults (not intended for children under 3)

dosing.start: Children 3–12 years (15–40 kg): 0.5 mg/day. Adults: 0.5–2 mg two or three times daily (moderate symptoms).
dosing.target: Children: increase by 0.5 mg every 5–7 days to 0.05–0.075 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses
dosing.max: Not specified for Tourette's; individualize to the lowest effective dose
dosing.notes: Adult dosing in the label is general (not Tourette-specific). Monitor for EPS, tardive dyskinesia, QT prolongation, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

boxedWarnings: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis
contraindications: Severe toxic CNS depression or comatose states
approved.plainSummary: An older antipsychotic that can strongly reduce tics, but it often causes stiffness, restlessness, or other movement side effects.

verified.note: Indication, pediatric Tourette dosing, boxed warning, and contraindications confirmed on the generic label (8/2026). The adult starting range is from the label's general adult dosing and was not re-read in full; original approval year for Tourette's not confirmed. Drugs@FDA lists all Haldol oral NDAs as discontinued.

approved.indication: Suppression of motor and phonic tics in patients with Tourette's Disorder who have failed to respond satisfactorily to standard treatment; not a first-choice treatment and reserved for patients whose development or daily functioning is severely compromised by tics.

population.ages: Efficacy trials enrolled ages 8–53 (most 12 or older); label provides pediatric dosing but data under 12 are limited

dosing.start: Adults: 1–2 mg/day in divided doses. Children: 0.05 mg/kg once at bedtime.
dosing.target: Adults: increase every other day; most maintained below 0.2 mg/kg/day or 10 mg/day. Children: increase every third day.
dosing.max: 0.2 mg/kg/day or 10 mg/day, whichever is less
dosing.notes: Baseline and periodic ECG. CYP2D6 genotyping required above 4 mg/day (adults) or 0.05 mg/kg/day (children); in poor metabolizers do not exceed 4 mg/day or 0.05 mg/kg/day and wait at least 14 days between increases. Many CYP3A4-inhibitor and QT-drug interactions.

contraindications: Simple tics or tics not associated with Tourette's Disorder
Patients taking drugs that may cause tics (e.g., methylphenidate, amphetamines) until withdrawn
Congenital long QT, history of arrhythmias, other QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia
Severe toxic CNS depression or comatose states
Macrolide antibiotics and other strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (see label for full list)
approved.plainSummary: An older antipsychotic used only for severe tics when other treatments fail; it needs heart tracings (ECGs) because it can affect heart rhythm.

verified.note: Indication, dosing, CYP2D6 rules, and contraindications 1–5 confirmed on the generic label (8/2026); the full list of interacting drugs in contraindication 6 onward was not read in full. No boxed warning section is present on this label. Approval year (Orap, 1984) not confirmed from a primary source. Drugs@FDA lists Orap (NDA 017473) as discontinued.

offLabel.notes: The AAN 2019 guideline lists alpha-2 agonists as an option, with better evidence when ADHD co-occurs. An RCT in children with tics and ADHD showed tic reduction; a later trial of guanfacine ER for tics alone was negative. Sedation, hypotension, bradycardia; taper to avoid rebound hypertension.

references.label: Pringsheim T et al. AAN practice guideline: treatment of tics in Tourette syndrome and chronic tic disorders. Neurology 2019 (PMID 31061208)
Scahill L et al. Placebo-controlled study of guanfacine in children with tic disorders and ADHD. Am J Psychiatry 2001 (PMID 11431228)

offLabel.notes: Named by the AAN guideline. In the Tourette's Syndrome Study Group trial, clonidine (alone or with methylphenidate) improved ADHD symptoms and tics did not worsen. Sedation is common; monitor blood pressure and heart rate; avoid abrupt discontinuation.

references.label: Pringsheim T et al. AAN practice guideline: treatment of tics. Neurology 2019 (PMID 31061208)
Tourette's Syndrome Study Group. Treatment of ADHD in children with tics: RCT. Neurology 2002 (PMID 11865128)

offLabel.notes: Listed in the AAN guideline among antipsychotics with evidence for tic reduction. Weight gain, metabolic effects, hyperprolactinemia, sedation, and EPS.

references.label: Pringsheim T et al. AAN practice guideline: treatment of tics. Neurology 2019 (PMID 31061208)

offLabel.notes: One small RCT (about 30 patients) showed tic reduction; the AAN guideline rates evidence as low. Cognitive slowing, paresthesia, weight loss, kidney stones.

references.label: Jankovic J et al. RCT of topiramate in Tourette syndrome. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2010 (PMID 19726418)
